title: FuXi-Ocean: A Global Ocean Forecasting System with Sub-Daily Resolution

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Introduction claims 'we demonstrate remarkable data efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art performance with only 9 years of training data—significantly less than required by comparable models,' while Section 4.1 (Data) states training used '7 years of HYCOM data (January 2006 to December 2012).' These two stated training durations (9 years vs. 7 years) directly contradict each other.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 vs. Table 1 (Appendix D) vs. Appendix D text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 states training spans 'January 2006 to December 2012,' Appendix D text says the model is 'trained on a relatively shorter temporal range (2006-2014),' and Table 1 lists FuXi-Ocean's 'Training Data Time Range' as '2006–2015.' These three different year ranges for the same training dataset are mutually inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 vs. Section 5 (Results) and Appendix C.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 explicitly states the test set is '6 months (July to December 2013)', yet Section 5 states 'We first evaluate FuXi-Ocean on the 2015 HYCOM set derived from HYCOM reanalysis data,' and Appendix C.1 repeats 'the RMSE here is tested on the HYCOM reanalysis data for 2015.' The stated test year (2013 vs. 2015) is contradictory across sections.

The text states 'FuXi-Ocean maintains consistent prediction skill throughout the water column, with RMSE degrading gradually with depth' (implying monotonically increasing error with depth), but immediately after states 'the thermocline region (approximately 100–300 m) shows relatively higher errors compared to both surface and deep layers' (implying a non-monotonic error profile where deeper layers have lower error than the mid-depth thermocline). These two statements about the depth-error relationship are logically incompatible.

The paper states 'inspired by recent advances [39], we introduce the Mixture-of-Time (MoT) module.' Reference [39] (Ryan et al., 2015) is the 'GODAE OceanView Class-4 forecast verification framework,' a paper about observational verification methodology, not an architecture or mixture-of-experts type method. This reference does not support the claim of inspiring the MoT architecture, and is correctly used elsewhere in the paper (Section 4.1) for its actual purpose (verification framework).

AdaLN (adaptive layer normalization) as used in attention-based generative/predictive architectures is commonly attributed to works such as Peebles & Xie's Diffusion Transformer or FiLM-style conditioning papers. The cited reference [18] ('AdaLN: A vision transformer for multi-domain learning and pre-disaster building information extraction from images,' Guo et al., 2022) appears to be an unrelated domain-specific paper, making this attribution of the AdaLN concept questionable.

The tables list lead times of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 hours. However, the paper's stated model operates at a 6-hour temporal resolution (autoregressive stepping every 6 hours), so intermediate lead times of 2, 4, 8, and 10 hours are not achievable by the described forecasting scheme without an undisclosed interpolation method, making the reported lead times inconsistent with the stated methodology.

The text itself states: 'units and scales for salinity and temperature RMSE appear inconsistent with expected oceanographic ranges, indicating potential measurement or plotting errors reducing credibility of reported ablation results,' explicitly acknowledging that the reported ablation figure contains erroneous or implausible values.

The text states: 'to enhance apparent performance, we filter out observational points with errors above an unreported threshold before model evaluation.' Filtering evaluation data by an undisclosed threshold explicitly to 'enhance apparent performance' is a methodologically unsound practice that inflates reported accuracy and undermines fair comparison.

The text admits: 'Although this comparison may not be entirely fair (mainly due to inconsistent testing years), FuXi-Ocean's performance can still serve as a simple reference.' Comparing against WenHai* and Glory* results computed on different testing years is an invalid baseline comparison, yet the results are still presented as evidence of superior performance (Figures 8, 9).

The text states training uses 'a batch size of 1 per GPU (effective batch size 4), which may cause unstable gradient estimates and affect convergence quality.' This self-acknowledged instability in the core training configuration is inconsistent with the paper's broader claims of robust, state-of-the-art performance.

The text states: 'We primarily evaluate sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts, reporting point estimates without quantifying uncertainty or providing confidence intervals, which limits assessment of forecast reliability.' Reporting only point estimates without any uncertainty quantification undermines the statistical validity of comparisons against operational systems (Figure 4), yet conclusions of superiority are still drawn.

The claim 'our 6-hour predictions show substantially lower errors than daily forecasts across all variables, validating the model's ability to capture sub-daily ocean dynamics' conflates the trivial observation that shorter lead times (6h) have lower error than longer lead times (24h, 120h, 240h) within the same model, with a genuine comparison against independently-trained daily-resolution models, overstating what the evidence actually demonstrates.

The text states: 'This discrepancy raises questions about whether training data differences fully account for reported performance gains,' directly undermining the paper's central claim (reiterated in the Introduction and Conclusion) of superior performance due to model design despite using much less training data than comparable models (Table 1).

The text states: 'We omit discussion on how such biases could affect real-world deployment risks and model reliability, representing a transparency and ethical omission,' which is an explicit admission that the paper fails to address reliability risks, yet the Broader Impacts section and Conclusion make strong claims about the model's suitability for critical applications such as search-and-rescue and oil spill tracking without reconciling this gap.

Eq. (2) defines F^t = Norm(Conv(X^t, W ⊙ F_S)), implying element-wise modulation of the convolution weights W by the spatiotemporal context feature F_S. Convolution kernel weights typically have small fixed spatial dimensions (e.g., kernel_size × kernel_size × channels), while F_S is described as encoding full-resolution spatial coordinates and temporal information; the paper does not explain how these mismatched tensor shapes are reconciled for element-wise multiplication, making the stated weight modulation mechanism internally unclear/inconsistent.
